# Validation Report: Cross-Checking Ten Widely Repeated Claims Against Retrieved Wikipedia Content

**Report date:** 2026-09-26
**Method:** Each claim was dispatched to a dedicated research agent for retrieval and cross-check against the relevant Wikipedia articles. Verdicts below reflect only what the retrieved content actually supports. Numbered citations refer to the source list at the end.

---

## Validation Summary Table

| # | Claim | Verdict | Key Evidence |
|---|-------|---------|--------------|
| 1 | Humans use only 10% of their brains | **REFUTED** | Neuroimaging, lesion studies, metabolic cost [1][4] |
| 2 | The Great Wall is visible from space/the Moon | **REFUTED** | Astronaut accounts; hair-from-3-km analogy [2][3] |
| 3 | Einstein failed mathematics in school | **REFUTED** | Matura record: top grade (6) in math/physics [5][7] |
| 4 | Goldfish have a 3-second memory | **REFUTED** | Documented span of ≥3 months, up to a year [8] |
| 5 | Napoleon was unusually short | **UNVERIFIED** | Retrieval returned no substantive content — see §Limitations |
| 6 | The tongue map (distinct taste zones) is accurate | **REFUTED** | Bartoshuk 1993; all tastes detected in all bud-bearing regions [9][11] |
| 7 | People swallow 8 spiders a year while sleeping | **REFUTED / ORIGIN ITSELF UNVERIFIED** | No evidence; "Lisa Holst" citation likely fabricated [12][13] |
| 8 | Sugar causes hyperactivity in children | **REFUTED** | Wolraich 1995 JAMA meta-analysis of 16 double-blind trials [14] |
| 9 | Vikings wore horned helmets in battle | **REFUTED** | Gjermundbu helmet hornless; Doepler 1876 origin [15][16][17] |
| 10 | Hair and nails keep growing after death | **REFUTED** | Mitosis requires circulation; skin desiccation illusion [18][19] |

---

## Claim-by-Claim Validation

### Claim 1 — "We use only 10% of our brains" → REFUTED
The Wikipedia article "Ten percent of the brain myth" traces the figure to Lowell Thomas's 1936 preface to Dale Carnegie's book ("the average person develops only 10 percent of his latent mental ability"), with earlier seeds in William James's 1907 *The Energies of Men* — which referred to untapped potential, not literal brain usage — and a misreading of Karl Lashley's rat-lesion experiments [1]. The refutation is corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence: fMRI/PET activity across the whole brain, identified function for every region, deficits from damage to virtually any area, the brain's ~2%-of-body-weight / ~20%-of-energy cost, and atrophy of chronically unused neurons [1][4]. The Einstein-attribution variant has no supporting evidence [1]. **Status: the refutation is well supported by the retrieved content.**

### Claim 2 — "The Great Wall is visible from space/the Moon" → REFUTED
The retrieved content is internally consistent across two Wikipedia articles. The physical argument (a 6–9 m wide structure viewed from ~384,400 km is equivalent to seeing a human hair from 3 km) aligns with the "List of common misconceptions" entry stating no man-made object is visible from the Moon unaided [2][3]. Astronaut testimony converges: Yang Liwei could not see it; William Pogue saw only the Grand Canal unaided and the wall only with binoculars; Leroy Chiao photographed it without confirming naked-eye sighting; Gene Cernan's claim of visibility from 100–200 miles is flagged as an outlier [2]. The myth's pre-space-age origins (Stukeley 1754, Norman 1895, Halliburton 1938) are documented [3]. **Status: refutation validated; one dissenting account (Cernan) properly noted rather than suppressed.**

### Claim 3 — "Einstein failed math" → REFUTED
The retrieved record contradicts the claim at every stage: self-taught algebra and geometry at 12, calculus mastered by 15, exceptional physics/math scores on the failed 1895 ETH entrance exam (he failed only the non-science portion), and a top grade of 6 in mathematics and physics on the 1896 Matura [5]. The origin is plausibly explained by grading-scale confusion — 6 was the *highest* Swiss mark, but reads as failing in the German system — plus a 1935 *Ripley's Believe It or Not!* item that prompted Einstein's written rebuttal: "I never failed in mathematics" [5][7]. **Status: refutation validated; the kernel of truth (the 1895 entrance exam) is correctly identified.**

### Claim 4 — "Goldfish have a 3-second memory" → REFUTED
Wikipedia's goldfish article states a memory span of **at least three months**, with the fish intelligence article citing evidence of retention up to a year or more, including Plymouth University lever-pressing experiments and Kevin Warburton's (Charles Sturt University) fish-cognition studies [8]. **Status: refutation validated**, though the agent noted that specific study attributions may shift between Wikipedia revisions — the core "≥3 months" figure is stable.

### Claim 5 — "Napoleon was unusually short" → ⚠️ UNVERIFIED
**This claim could not be validated in this run.** The research agent executed the correct queries ("Napoleon Bonaparte Wikipedia height," "Napoleon height 5 feet 2 inches French units," "Napoleon short myth average Frenchman height") but retrieved no substantive content — only the query log was returned. Per validation protocol, no verdict is assigned and no figures are supplied from memory. **Recommendation: re-run this subtopic before relying on the report.** The general pattern of the other nine claims (French/English unit confusion as a myth origin) would predict a "myth" verdict, but that inference is *not* evidence and is not counted here.

### Claim 6 — "The tongue map is accurate" → REFUTED
The retrieved content traces the map to David Paul Hänig's 1901 threshold study, which found only *slight* sensitivity variations that Edwin G. Boring (1942) exaggerated into discrete zones in his plotting [9][10]. Modern evidence: all five basic tastes are detectable in every region containing taste buds (Bartoshuk 1993), individual receptor cells respond to multiple taste qualities, and taste buds exist beyond the tongue (soft palate, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx) — which the classic map omits entirely [9][11]. **Status: refutation validated, with the legitimate nuance that minor regional threshold differences do exist.**

### Claim 7 — "People swallow 8 spiders a year in their sleep" → REFUTED, with a notable twist
The retrieved content rates the claim an urban legend with no factual basis: spiders perceive sleeping humans as predators and are deterred by heartbeat/breathing/snoring vibrations; arachnologist Rod Crawford argues swallowing even one live spider is practically ruled out [12][13]. Critically, the commonly cited origin — columnist "Lisa Holst," *PC Professional*, 1993 — **has never been verified to exist**, making this a "myth about a myth" whose true origin is unknown [12][13]. **Status: the claim is refuted, but the validation also correctly declines to assert a confident origin story.**

### Claim 8 — "Sugar causes hyperactivity" → REFUTED
The retrieved evidence centers on the Wolraich, Wilson & White 1995 *JAMA* meta-analysis of 16 double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (23 comparisons), finding no significant effect on behavior or cognition — including in ADHD subgroups and children whose parents believed them sugar-sensitive [14]. The Hoover & Milich (1994) experiment isolates the mechanism: mothers told their sons had consumed sugar (actually a placebo) rated them as more hyperactive — expectation bias, not sugar [14]. Situational confounding (birthday parties, Halloween) is noted as reinforcing the illusion [14]. **Status: refutation validated with a clearly identified causal explanation for the myth's persistence.**

### Claim 9 — "Vikings wore horned helmets" → REFUTED
Archaeology is decisive: the only complete Viking Age helmet, the Gjermundbu helmet (Ringerike, Norway, c. 970, found 1943), is a hornless rounded iron cap with a spectacle visor; the Tjele fragment is likewise hornless [15][16][17]. The horned *Veksø* helmets are Bronze Age (c. 900 BC) — roughly 1,500 years before the Viking Age — and are frequently misattributed [17]. The popular image is traced to 19th-century Romantic nationalism and, decisively, Carl Emil Doepler's 1876 costume designs for the Bayreuth premiere of Wagner's *Ring des Nibelungen* [15][16]. **Status: refutation validated; the retrieved content is consistent across the "Horned helmet," "Viking Age," "Gjermundbu," and "Veksø" articles, plus the National Museum of Denmark.**

### Claim 10 — "Hair and nails grow after death" → REFUTED
The retrieved content confirms the biological impossibility: hair and nail growth require continuous mitosis in the matrix tissues, fueled by circulating oxygen and glucose, which cease at death [18][19]. The *appearance* of growth is explained by skin desiccation — drying skin retracts around the nail beds and face, exposing already-existing shafts and plates, typically within days [18]. The folklore pedigree (Remarque's *All Quiet on the Western Front*) is documented [18]. **Status: refutation validated with a complete mechanistic explanation.**

---

## Reliability Assessment

**Strengths of the validation:**
- **Internal consistency:** Where multiple Wikipedia articles cover the same claim (Great Wall: article + misconceptions list; Vikings: four separate articles), the retrieved content agrees without contradiction.
- **Origin claims are properly hedged:** Two claims (10% brain, spiders) have *unknown or unverifiable* origins, and the validation correctly marks these as such rather than asserting popular-but-unverified origin stories (e.g., the fabricated "Lisa Holst" citation).
- **Kernels of truth preserved:** The 1895 Einstein entrance exam, Bronze Age Veksø helmets, and minor tongue-sensitivity gradients are retained as context — the refutations are precise, not overbroad.

**Limitations and caveats:**
1. **Claim 5 (Napoleon) is unvalidated** — the subtopic returned only search queries with no retrieved content. No verdict should be inferred.
2. Several research agents noted they could not perform live page fetches and relied on retrieved snippets/session knowledge; specific figures (e.g., "~86 billion" neurons [4]; exact study attributions in the goldfish article [8]) should be treated as consistent-with but not byte-verified against current Wikipedia revisions.
3. All citations resolve to Wikipedia articles and the primary literature those articles cite (James 1907, Beyerstein 1999, Hänig 1901, Bartoshuk 1993, Wolraich 1995, etc.); for publication-grade use, the primary sources should be pulled directly.

---

## Sources

1. Wikipedia, "Ten percent of the brain myth"
2. Wikipedia, "Great Wall of China," § "Visibility from space"
3. Wikipedia, "List of common misconceptions"
4. Beyerstein, B. "Whence Cometh the Myth that We Only Use 10% of our Brains?" in Della Sala (ed.), *Mind Myths* (1999); Azevedo et al., *J. Comp. Neurol.* (2009)
5. Wikipedia, "Albert Einstein," § "Early life and education"
6. Wikipedia, "Albert Einstein in popular culture"
7. Calaprice, A. (ed.), *The Ultimate Quotable Einstein*, Princeton UP (2011)
8. Wikipedia, "Goldfish" and "Fish intelligence"; Plymouth University lever studies; Warburton, K. (Charles Sturt University)
9. Wikipedia, "Tongue map"
10. Hänig, D.P. (1901). "Zur Psychophysik des Geschmackssinnes." *Philosophische Studien* 17; Boring, E.G. (1942). *Sensation and Perception in the History of Experimental Psychology*
11. Bartoshuk, L.M. (1993). *Food Quality and Preference* 4; Lindemann, B. (2001). *Nature* 413; Smith & Margolskee (2001). *Scientific American* 284(3)
12. Wikipedia, "Swallowing spiders"
13. Crawford, R., Burke Museum "Spider Myths"; Radford, B., *Skeptical Inquirer*; Snopes.com
14. Wikipedia, "Sugar" (health effects); Wolraich, Wilson & White (1995). *JAMA*; Hoover & Milich (1994). *J. Abnorm. Child Psychol.*
15. Wikipedia, "Horned helmet"
16. Wikipedia, "Viking Age"; National Museum of Denmark, "The Viking helmet that never was"
17. Wikipedia, "Gjermundbu helmet"; Wikipedia, "Veksø helmets"
18. Wikipedia, "List of common misconceptions" (postmortem growth entry); Wikipedia, "Decomposition"
19. Wikipedia, "Hair"

**Bottom line:** Nine of ten claims are refuted with strong, internally consistent support from the retrieved Wikipedia content; one (Napoleon's height) failed retrieval and remains unvalidated. Citation numbering above is assigned per the source list and should be preserved verbatim in any downstream use of this report.
